Hold on and sound all the way past it
Alter to clear it by 1 M more than planned

10°, for her high topsides and flybridge

12.0 M to windward of the EP

At the turn to foul, when it is slack
On the first estimate, with no margin

Trust the EP and leave the fix off the chart
Plot the midpoint of the two and carry on

Work the EP from the last fix as well

fig.title: Pilot boards at the fairway buoy, 0800
lines: Foul stream 1.5 kn all the way

q: You must catch up with the sister yacht ahead to pass her a spare part. How long until you are alongside?
why: Same course, so you close at 8.5 − 6.0 = 2.5 kn: 24.0 ÷ 2.5 = 9.6 h = 9 h 36.
ref: Course to steer — a rendezvous at sea

fig.title: Sister yacht 24.0 M ahead, same course
lines: Open sea, the same current for both

q: Your sister yacht radios her position for a night rendezvous. Which course and distance close her?
why: d.lat 30.0' N; d.long 45.0' E × cos 46°25' = 31.0 M of departure: 046°T, 43.2 M. Not 45 M of d.long as miles.
ref: Course to steer — a rendezvous at sea

fig.title: Rendezvous by radio
lines: She lies hove-to, waiting for you

q: At night in the north-east-bound lane, the plotter shows you set towards the separation zone, with the bend ahead. What do you do?
a: Regain the lane's track and follow it round the bend
o: Steer straight for the next waypoint from here
Hold the heading: 0.6 M is still inside the lane
Reset the route so that the XTE reads zero
why: In a lane a new course to the waypoint cuts the corner through the separation zone; get back on the planned track.
ref: Cross-track error — in a TSS lane

fig.note: Night · XTE 0.6 M towards the zone · sketch

q: The stream is setting you across the lane towards the separation zone. Which heading regains the lane's track within 3 M?
why: Close 0.6 M in 3.0 M: ground track 045° + 11° = 056°T. Against 1.2 kn toward 315°T at 7.5 kn, head 9° more to starboard: 065°T.
ref: Cross-track error — in a TSS lane

fig.title: NE-bound lane, 0300
lines: XTE 0.6 M to port, towards the zone

q: In the lane, with a strong stream across it, you engage the autopilot's track mode on the route. What does it do?
a: Heads up into the stream to hold the track line
o: Holds the heading it had and lets her drift off
Points the bow at the waypoint, stream or not
Switches itself off once the XTE grows
why: Track mode steers to keep the XTE near zero, so it crabs into the stream; heading and COG differ.
ref: Cross-track error — in a TSS lane

fig.title: TSS lane, night
lines: Route leg runs down the lane centre

q: You compare six hours of GNSS track with the log and the heading. What current has set you?
why: Water track 237°T (leeway 3° to port), 46.8 M. Ground 51.0 M on 228°T less that: 8.7 M toward 171°T in 6 h = 1.5 kn.

fig.title: Six hours, 0000–0600
lines: GNSS fix to fix: 51.0 M toward 228°T

q: Mid-ocean, the GNSS and the log disagree steadily along your heading for six hours. What can you conclude?
a: A fair current, a log that under-reads, or both
o: A fair current of 1.0 kn, for certain
A GNSS error: trust the log instead
why: A difference along the heading can be current or log error; you can't split them without a log check or a cross-track sign.

fig.title: Six steady hours
lines: Log last calibrated at the start of the season

q: You stop the engines of your motor yacht to change a fuel filter in a flat calm. What current is running?
why: Stopped in a calm, the drift is the current: 0.9 M in 40 min = 0.9 ÷ 0.67 h = 1.4 kn toward 075°T.

fig.title: Engines stopped 0300–0340
lines: Flat calm, no wind on the hull

q: After 15 hours the current turns out to have run in a different direction from the one in your EP. Where is the yacht against the EP?
why: Real minus used: 12 M on 210°T less 12 M on 180°T = 6.2 M toward 285°T. The same rate still moves you 2 × 12 × sin 15°.
ref: DR — error growth on a long passage

q: You crossed on one course worked from the spring rates, but today is neaps. If all else is right, where do you end up?
why: You aimed off for 9.6 M of east-going stream; neaps gave only 55%, 5.3 M. The other 4.3 M of aim-off leaves you west, up-tide.
ref: DR — error growth on a long passage

fig.title: Crossing to B, 8 h, one heading
lines: Today is neaps: rates 55% of springs
No leeway, log and steering good

q: Your ETA is worked from the log speed, but the log was found to under-read. When do you really arrive, if the speed holds?
ref: DR — error growth on a long passage

fig.title: Log check on a measured run

q: After 144 M of open sea your EP will be rough, so you plan to hit the low coast well north of the harbour. What do you lay off from the direct line?
why: 1 in 60: 9 M off over 144 M is 9 × 60 ÷ 144 ≈ 4°, to the side you chose. The 6 M of doubt alone gives too little.

fig.title: Landfall plan
lines: Harbour 144 M ahead on a low coast
EP doubt ±6 M across the track
Plan: strike the coast 9 M north of it

q: You want to strike the coast 6 M north of the harbour, with this current across your track all the way. Which heading do you steer?
why: The current sets you 12 M north in 20 h; you want only 6 M: 6 M to cancel, 6 × 60 ÷ 120 = 3° south of 090°T, 093°T.

q: Your passage runs well outside the area of the tidal stream atlas. What stream data do you use out there?
a: The current from the routeing chart, checked by fixes
o: The arrows from the atlas's nearest page
None: there is no stream at all offshore
The plotter's tidal arrows from the coast
why: Offshore the tidal streams are weak and rotary; the routeing (pilot) chart gives the mean current. Check it by fixes.

fig.title: 120 M west of the shelf edge
lines: The tidal stream atlas ends 40 M offshore

q: At 0215 the whole electrical system dies. From the paper log, where is your DR from the 2300 fix?
why: 205°C + 2°E − 7°W = 200°T for 15.6 M; 228°C + 6°E − 7°W = 227°T for 9.7 M: 210°T, 24.6 M. Each heading has its deviation.

fig.title: Rebuilding the DR · var 7°W
lines: Running before the wind · no stream

q: With the electrics dead you need a speed for the DR, so you time a chip of wood along the deck. What speed do you log?

fig.title: No log, no GNSS
lines: Two marks on deck 22.0 m apart
A chip thrown at the bow passes them

q: At 0240 every instrument and the autopilot go dark. What gives you the heading for the DR from now on?
a: The magnetic steering compass, read by torchlight
o: The heading the plotter showed before it died
The COG of a handheld GNSS, taken as the heading
why: The magnetic compass needs no power; steer and log by it, applying its deviation. COG is not heading.

fig.title: 0240: total electrical failure
lines: Steering by hand from now on
Handheld GNSS on its own batteries

q: Your motor yacht lay stopped for repairs after the fix, beam-on to the wind. Where is the 0400 EP from the 0130 fix?
why: 2 h 30 = 2.5 h: windage 3.0 M toward 110°T plus current 1.5 M toward 200°T: 137°T, 3.4 M. 2 h 30 is not 2.3 h.

q: You run due west along the parallel for a day with no current. What is tomorrow's noon DR longitude?
